q: Which substance has the chemical formula H₂O?
fact: Water is one of the few substances that expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.

q: At what temperature in Celsius does water freeze?
fact: Adding salt to water lowers its freezing point, which is why roads are gritted with salt in winter.

q: Which force keeps our feet on the ground?
fact: On the Moon, gravity is about a sixth as strong, so you'd weigh about a sixth of what you do on Earth.

q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
fact: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times every day.

q: Which organs do we use to breathe?
fact: Your left lung is slightly smaller than your right, which leaves room for your heart.

q: Which gas do we need to breathe in to stay alive?
fact: Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air we breathe.

q: What does a thermometer measure?
fact: Normal human body temperature is about 37°C.

q: How many colours are traditionally listed in a rainbow?
fact: You can only see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and the rain is in front of you.

q: Which of these metals does a magnet attract?
fact: The Earth itself acts like a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.

q: Which bone protects your brain?
fact: A newborn baby's skull has soft gaps called fontanelles, which close up as they grow.

q: What would you use to look at tiny things like cells?
fact: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was among the first to see bacteria, using tiny home-made microscopes in the 1670s.

q: Light bulbs are labelled with their power in which unit?
fact: The watt is named after James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine.

q: Which vitamin does your skin make when it's in sunlight?
fact: Oily fish such as salmon and mackerel are among the few foods naturally rich in vitamin D.

q: What do solar panels turn sunlight into?
fact: Solar panels still make some electricity on cloudy days, just less than in full sunshine.

q: Which gas makes the bubbles in fizzy drinks?
fact: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water forms a weak acid, giving fizzy drinks their slight tang.

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
fact: Red blood cells get their colour from haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein.

q: What is the hard, white outer layer of a tooth called?
fact: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.

q: Which organs clean your blood and make urine?
fact: Most people have two kidneys, but you can live a healthy life with just one.

q: Which direction does a compass needle point?
fact: A compass points to magnetic north, which isn't quite the same place as the North Pole.

q: What is an echo?
fact: Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their way and hunt, a skill called echolocation.

q: Which of these travels fastest?
fact: Light travels so much faster than sound that you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

q: Sodium chloride is better known as what?
fact: Sodium on its own is a soft metal that reacts violently with water.

q: What is a scientist who studies rocks called?
fact: The word 'geology' comes from the Greek words for 'Earth' and 'study'.

q: Bread, rice and pasta are rich in which nutrient?
fact: Your body breaks carbohydrates down into glucose, its main source of quick energy.

q: Which joint connects your hand to your arm?
fact: Each wrist contains eight small bones called carpals.

q: Which force slows down an object sliding across a surface?
fact: Rubbing your hands together warms them up because friction turns movement into heat.

q: What is a material that lets electricity flow easily called?
fact: Plastic is an insulator, which is why electrical wires are wrapped in it.

q: Which metal are most household electrical wires made of?
fact: Of all metals, only silver conducts electricity better than copper.

q: Steam, or water vapour, is water in which state?
fact: True steam is invisible: the white cloud above a kettle is really tiny water droplets.

q: Which scientist is famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
fact: Darwin's ideas were shaped by his voyage on HMS Beagle, including a visit to the Galápagos Islands.

q: What is it called when water slowly turns into vapour, like a drying puddle?
fact: Puddles dry up faster on warm, windy days because evaporation speeds up.

q: In which part of the body would you find the retina?
fact: Images land on the retina upside down, and your brain flips them the right way up.

q: In a school science lab, what is a Bunsen burner used for?
fact: The Bunsen burner is named after German chemist Robert Bunsen, who helped make it popular in the 1850s.

q: Which gas is used to make party balloons float?
fact: Helium is the second most common element in the universe, after hydrogen.

q: Taste buds are mostly found on which part of your body?
fact: Your taste buds are constantly renewed, with each one lasting only a week or two.
